syllabus.clause: leveled vs tiered (universal) vs hybrid compaction, and the read/write/space amplification trade-off (RUM conjecture). Compaction must be budgeted against foreground I/O and CPU (rate limiting, write stalls).

at.step: Measured: the run count genuinely kept growing
Measured: both leveled and tiered compaction genuinely beat no compaction at all, on both read and space amplification
Measured: leveled and tiered compaction genuinely cost different amounts of rewritten data on the identical workload, with tiered costing less
Measured: the tiered compactor that cost less rewritten data genuinely left more files to check and more stale data on disk than leveled did

items.item: this sacrifices write amplification by one but may significantly improve read amplification in L0 and in turn increase the capability RocksDB can hold data in L0

items.item: universal compaction style is a compaction style, targeting the use cases requiring lower write amplification, trading off read amplification and space amplification

items.item: The no-compaction baseline and both real compactors are fed the identical sequence of batches, built by the same workload() function, so every comparison between them is a genuine apples-to-apples measurement rather than an artifact of different inputs.

at.step: Measured: both leveled and tiered compaction genuinely beat no compaction at all, on both read and space amplification

items.item: The write-amplification claim counts every input entry actually processed by every merge a strategy performs, including entries from a level's or tier's own pre-existing run being re-merged, so the measured cost reflects real re-rewriting, not just the entries newly flushed.

at.step: Measured: leveled and tiered compaction genuinely cost different amounts of rewritten data on the identical workload, with tiered costing less

items.item: The read/space-amplification claim is checked at the same point in the identical workload for both strategies (after all twenty batches), not at an arbitrarily convenient moment for either one, so the measured difference reflects the strategies' own structural trade-off rather than a lucky or unlucky snapshot.

at.step: Measured: the tiered compactor that cost less rewritten data genuinely left more files to check and more stale data on disk than leveled did

items.item: The workload deliberately overwrites every one of its fifty distinct keys in full on every single batch, so every merge's deduplication step has real, verifiable work to do; a workload of only ever-new keys would never exercise the deduplication this topic's own claims depend on.

at.step: Flush memtables to SSTables over and over, with no compaction at all. As more and more flushes pile up, does a lookup's own cost ever stop growing?

items.item: This topic's own leveled compactor is a simplified, two-level cascade (not RocksDB's own multi-level, multi-file-per-level design) and its own tiered compactor merges every current run at once rather than RocksDB's own size-ratio-triggered subset merges; both are real, working, measurably different compaction policies built for this topic's own claims, not a claim to replicate RocksDB's exact algorithms.

at.step: Run a real leveled compactor and a real tiered compactor against that same pile of flushes instead. Do both of them at least beat doing no compaction at all, on how many files a lookup has to check and how much stale data sits on disk?

items.item: This topic continues directly from topic 56's own lsm-write-read-amplification-paths id, since the SSTables this topic's own compactors merge are exactly the structures topic 56's own flush path produces.

at.step: Flush memtables to SSTables over and over, with no compaction at all. As more and more flushes pile up, does a lookup's own cost ever stop growing?

items.item: The syllabus names the RUM conjecture (read, update, and memory overhead can't all be minimized at once) directly; this topic's own measured write-versus-read/space trade-off between tiered and leveled compaction is a concrete instance of exactly that conjecture, not a separate, unrelated measurement.

at.step: Measured: the tiered compactor that cost less rewritten data genuinely left more files to check and more stale data on disk than leveled did

items.item: All of this topic's own measured claims run entirely on in-memory Rust collections with no file, network, or root access needed, continuing this chapter's own established pattern from topic 56.
